messages.author: 127cc61ff89e630a
messages.subject: Multi-session likelihood questions
parts:
Hi, 
I am looking for clarification on the multi-session likelihood in oSCR. I'm finding very different abundance estimates across model specifications and I want to make sure that I'm interpreting correctly what is happening under the hood. Below is pseudo code for each fitted model and the accompanying (real) Nhat estimates from predict.oSCR for each. The SCR frame is multi-session (3 years) and sex structured, with decent sample sizes. 
S1 S2 S3 n individuals 69 83 51 n traps 35 140 94 n occasions 3 6 3
n individuals 17 39 33
spatial recap

First, I specified the null model for density with the best model for p0, which to my understanding assumes constant density (both spatially and across sessions).
Model 1:D(~1) p(~effort_year + river_reach + curvsd_900m)sig(~sex) 
Using this model to predict abundance results in what appear to be session-specific predictions from predict.oSCR: 
Nhat: 191.5435
Nhat: 178.892
Nhat: 158.6549

I assume this is because predict.oSCR calculates a realization of the density point process for each session, regardless if session is specified in the model? If so, density is still assumed constant across sessions here and the differences in Nhat estimates across sessions are random and/or due to other unmodeled heterogeneity? 

Also, in this formulation, without session in the model, are spatial recaptures and detections across all years informing all parameters (so data are pooled across sessions for all params?)

Next, I specified a session-specific density model:
Model 2:D(~session) p(~effort_year + river_reach + curvsd_900m)sig(~sex) 

From the session-specific model,  abundance estimates across years are now drastically different for years 1 and 3, and potentially very wrong for year 1. But this model is strongly supported over Model 1 based on AIC. 
Nhat: 286.798
Nhat: 179.3723
Nhat: 127.2519

In this specification, because only density and no other params vary by session, are all detections and spatial recaptures still pooled to estimate params? OR, b/c density is now session specific, are the data no longer shared across sigma and p0, b/c of the hierarchical structure?  I ask b/c of the relatively fewer number of spatially recaptured animals in year 1 (17 of 69; 25%) compared to the subsequent 2 years and wonder if the large jump in abundance for session 1 compared to the constant model is bias due to the limited proportion of spatial recaps. 

For additional context, sampling effort and spatial coverage of sampling varied quite a bit each year. I have tried to account for this in the model for p0, but wonder if specifying a D~session model is not appropriate for these data given this result? 

Thanks very much in advance for any thoughts on this. 

Sarah

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: Multi-session likelihood questions
parts:
Hi Sarah,

These are good questions, and my quick answer is that you might need to fit a session-specific p0 model to compare with the others (assuming that "effort_year" is something else).

It's hard to say what is happening in your case without seeing a bit more info, particularly with regards to trap layout and effort.  It looks like there is a big difference between session 1 and session 2 in the number of traps.  And your detection model has some structure to it.  Assuming the state spaces are identical, if there is spatial variation in detection probability (given trap layout and effort) then it is not surprising for realized N to differ despite expected N (given constant density) to be the same.

It might be helpful to simulate some 3 session data with identical trap layout/effort and fit different combinations of session-specific parameters for D and p just to illustrate the concepts of what to expect, and then simulate again with layout/effort differences between sessions.

Variation in sampling effort and spatial coverage is not necessarily a problem, but it does potentially make it difficult for the model to partition variation between the density processes and the observation processes.  I would say that D~session models are never exactly "inappropriate" when sampling varies, but you might not have the power to estimate differences well.  One of the great things about spatial capture-recapture is that spatial variation in sampling effort is explicitly modeled and so even shoddy sampling designs can provide some inferences when there is enough data.  That said, nothing beats a well-executed sampling design!

messages.subject: Re: Multi-session likelihood questions
parts:
adding to Dan's comment, I will note that you captured way more individuals PER TRAP in session 1 than in sessions 2 and 3. Thus when you allow density to vary by session it has to reflect that structure in the data. I think even if, as Dan suggests, you allow p to vary by session also, you will have a similar results.
It seems  possible that the traps in session 1 are in a better habitat on average.

parts:
Hi Dan, Andy, and Chris, 

Thanks much for getting back. This does help me understand why I might be seeing that strong difference in abundance even with a D~1 model.  I should have clarified that I did already try p0~session and found the same result with regards to the density estimates... 'effort year' is essentially a more efficient version of "session" for p0 that separates year 1 from years 2-3 due to the pattern that Andy referred to (way more captures PER TRAP in year 1). The other covariate on p0 in these models is spatial and is an attempt to account for the spatial variation in sampling effort additively with "effort_year". I have not yet tried allowing the sex-ratio to vary, but as Dan mentioned, I am concerned that I might not have enough power to account for all the variation in the observation process as well as the ecological process for each year. 

Detection data come from pellet searches (bighorn sheep) in steep river canyons that were accessed from rivers on float trips and sites visited, etc. are pretty inconsistent across years. Some info on the data and trap layout attached if you're curious! I do think that simulations could be useful to understand the effects of the potential sampling design issues on results so thanks for that suggestion. 

 I'm also planning to fit the final model in a Bayesian context and have wondered if trying an alternative parameterization for p0 such as Poisson based on searched grid cells as in Milleret et al. (2018) could be a better fit given the sampling process. My main goal is to get a reasonably accurate estimation of abundance. 

Cheers, 
Sarah

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: [oscr] Re: Multi-session likelihood questions
parts:
Hi Sarah, this is great, thanks for sharing the details

I would say you have to be careful about using the encounter survey results to structure covariates.  If you don't have a great a priori reason for year 1 being different than years 2-3, it might be better to have detection be session-specific (or constant).  The layout of traps is spatially structured across time, such that 2019 seems to be a combination of Yampa and Green, while 2018 is mostly Green and 2020 is all Yampa.  It will be hard to partition variation into space vs time if the 2 are confounded by the design, so caution is warranted.

Is there a reason to think that river reach explains variation in detection as opposed to density?

Also, oSCR does allow for a Poisson encounter model, for what that's worth.

parts:
hi Sarah, 

thanks for the additional details. 

The highly linear structure of your system seems important, it might be worth thinking about how to build that structure into the model. (oSCR has a non-Euclidean distance modeling capability which requires a little bit of elbow grease to implement, you have to define cost surfaces and so forth).  Chris wrote a series of papers on this, e.g., Modelling non‐Euclidean movement and landscape connectivity in highly structured ecological networks - Sutherland - 2015 - Methods in Ecology and Evolution - Wiley Online Library

 At any rate I wonder a bit about the sampling method, whether this was based on formal a priori selection of units or whether folks just got in the boat and decided to sample where they knew scat would be selected and so on. Worth thinking about that too, if the study will continue.

regards
andy

On Thursday, December 7, 2023 at 6:33:56 PM UTC-5 slcarr...@gmail.com wrote:
Hi Dan, Andy, and Chris, 

Thanks much for getting back. This does help me understand why I might be seeing that strong difference in abundance even with a D~1 model.  I should have clarified that I did already try p0~session and found the same result with regards to the density estimates... 'effort year' is essentially a more efficient version of "session" for p0 that separates year 1 from years 2-3 due to the pattern that Andy referred to (way more captures PER TRAP in year 1). The other covariate on p0 in these models is spatial and is an attempt to account for the spatial variation in sampling effort additively with "effort_year". I have not yet tried allowing the sex-ratio to vary, but as Dan mentioned, I am concerned that I might not have enough power to account for all the variation in the observation process as well as the ecological process for each year. 

Detection data come from pellet searches (bighorn sheep) in steep river canyons that were accessed from rivers on float trips and sites visited, etc. are pretty inconsistent across years. Some info on the data and trap layout attached if you're curious! I do think that simulations could be useful to understand the effects of the potential sampling design issues on results so thanks for that suggestion. 

 I'm also planning to fit the final model in a Bayesian context and have wondered if trying an alternative parameterization for p0 such as Poisson based on searched grid cells as in Milleret et al. (2018) could be a better fit given the sampling process. My main goal is to get a reasonably accurate estimation of abundance. 

Cheers, 
Sarah 

On Thursday, December 7, 2023 at 8:22:12 AM UTC-7 Chris Sutherland wrote:
And then one last thing to add to both Dan and Andy’s comments is that there is assumption here that the sex-ratio parameter is constant (default: sexmod="constant"). If you are looking to allow for full flexibility, you might want to have the session-specific (sexmod="session").

adding to Dan's comment, I will note that you captured way more individuals PER TRAP in session 1 than in sessions 2 and 3. Thus when you allow density to vary by session it has to reflect that structure in the data. I think even if, as Dan suggests, you allow p to vary by session also, you will have a similar results.

It seems  possible that the traps in session 1 are in a better habitat on average.

 

On Tuesday, December 5, 2023 at 6:25:10 PM UTC-5 slcarr...@gmail.com wrote:

Hi, 

I am looking for clarification on the multi-session likelihood in oSCR. I'm finding very different abundance estimates across model specifications and I want to make sure that I'm interpreting correctly what is happening under the hood. Below is pseudo code for each fitted model and the accompanying (real) Nhat estimates from predict.oSCR for each. The SCR frame is multi-session (3 years) and sex structured, with decent sample sizes. 

S1 S2 S3 n individuals 69 83 51 n traps 35 140 94 n occasions 3 6 3

n individuals 17 39 33

spatial recap

 

First, I specified the null model for density with the best model for p0, which to my understanding assumes constant density (both spatially and across sessions).

Model 1:D(~1) p(~effort_year + river_reach + curvsd_900m)sig(~sex) 

Using this model to predict abundance results in what appear to be session-specific predictions from predict.oSCR: 

Nhat: 191.5435

Nhat: 178.892

Nhat: 158.6549

 

I assume this is because predict.oSCR calculates a realization of the density point process for each session, regardless if session is specified in the model? If so, density is still assumed constant across sessions here and the differences in Nhat estimates across sessions are random and/or due to other unmodeled heterogeneity? 

 

Also, in this formulation, without session in the model, are spatial recaptures and detections across all years informing all parameters (so data are pooled across sessions for all params?)

 

Next, I specified a session-specific density model:

Model 2:D(~session) p(~effort_year + river_reach + curvsd_900m)sig(~sex) 

 

From the session-specific model,  abundance estimates across years are now drastically different for years 1 and 3, and potentially very wrong for year 1. But this model is strongly supported over Model 1 based on AIC. 

Nhat: 286.798

Nhat: 179.3723

Nhat: 127.2519

 

In this specification, because only density and no other params vary by session, are all detections and spatial recaptures still pooled to estimate params? OR, b/c density is now session specific, are the data no longer shared across sigma and p0, b/c of the hierarchical structure?  I ask b/c of the relatively fewer number of spatially recaptured animals in year 1 (17 of 69; 25%) compared to the subsequent 2 years and wonder if the large jump in abundance for session 1 compared to the constant model is bias due to the limited proportion of spatial recaps. 

 

For additional context, sampling effort and spatial coverage of sampling varied quite a bit each year. I have tried to account for this in the model for p0, but wonder if specifying a D~session model is not appropriate for these data given this result? 

 

Thanks very much in advance for any thoughts on this. 

 

Sarah

parts:
Thanks Dan and Andy. 

With regard to the encounter model, we did know a priori that there was a different 'method' used to select pellets in the first year that resulted in higher genotyping success which is reflected in the encounter survey results discussed above and why we tried the effort_year covariate. Because of the spatial pattern in sampling, my thought was to try to account for variation due to that and the sampling method in p0 by with the additive model structure above (both the year and river reach sampled), but I think I see now that year and space would still be confounded even with this structure... I did also try a similar spatial covariate on density. It was moderately informative, but it if session was also in the mode for density, I obtained the same result of huge Nhat for 2018.   

Unfortunately the info I have on sampling methods is pretty thin, but as far as I know, sample sites were not chosen formally a priori and were more likely to be where it was physically possible to pull the boat over and get out and search for pellets. 

I am familiar with the papers Chris wrote on this and the cost-distance model as I used it in a previous study. I've considered it given the linear structure as well, but one thing that I thought might make applying it here tricky is that bighorn AC's can be anywhere /any distance from the river, but encountering was only possible near the river due to sampling design, and a given individual's AC is likely mostly river right or river left? Another thought I had is whether it might be best to omit one of the years of data (either 2018 or 2020) to address some of the sampling issues? 

Anyway, lots to think about, thanks!  

Sarah
